replacement.objective: Use an inside approach that guides Gold 1 away from the middle
replacement.briefing: Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. Gold 1 carries on the right side toward the blue line. YOU start inside; D1 is behind and Gold 2 is positioned wide.
cues: Gold 1 carries on the right side toward the blue line.

questions.prompt: Where is Gold 1 carrying?

options.text: Along the right side toward the blue line
Across the middle toward the left side

questions.explanation: Gold 1’s route gives YOU an inside angle to guide wide; a different route needs a different approach.

questions.prompt: Which two relationships fit the angling goal?

options.text: An approach that encourages a route toward the boards

questions.explanation: The drill aims to protect middle ice while retaining recovery. Board-side play is not automatically safe; support and pressure still matter.

questions.prompt: Order one angling approach.

options.text: Close from inside while matching the route
Recheck D1 and the changed carrier route

questions.explanation: Read the carrier, compare an inside approach and reassess with D1. No fixed finish is required.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare an approach nearer the middle and Navy’s net than Gold 1.
questions.explanation: The example stays inside and net-side of Gold 1, while reducing the gap. Recheck speed, Gold 2 and D1 before closing.

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 passes to Gold 2, what deserves attention?

options.text: Whether Gold 2 threatens middle and D1 can help
Angling the player who no longer has the puck

questions.explanation: The pass changes the puck threat. Reassess Gold 2 and agree responsibilities with D1.

questions.prompt: Why can a fast approach be unhelpful here?
questions.explanation: Speed without an inside angle can carry YOU past Gold 1 and give up middle, so match the route and keep support connected; if the carrier slows, close under control.

questions.prompt: Which attacker is the inside support threat?
questions.explanation: Gold 2 is nearer the middle than Gold 1. D1 is nearer the carrier, but completed coverage is not proved.

questions.prompt: Which two reads make your backcheck useful?
questions.explanation: The middle route identifies danger and D1’s position tells you whether to support inside; blind wide skating can miss the threat.

questions.prompt: Arrange one middle-lane backcheck.

options.text: Compare middle support while staying net-side

questions.explanation: Seeing Gold 2 prevents a puck-only chase; middle recovery protects net; communication avoids two defenders following Gold 1.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward the middle while remaining closer to Navy’s net than Gold 2.
questions.explanation: The example moves YOU toward the middle but farther from Navy’s net than the starting spot. It remains net-side of Gold 2; check speed and D1 before adjusting.

questions.prompt: If Gold 2 receives before you arrive, what changes?

options.text: Gold 2 becomes carrier and D1’s coverage must be reassessed
Your original route stays correct automatically
The net-side lane can be abandoned

questions.explanation: The reception changes the threat, so update carrier and roles; if Gold 2 is contained, recover to the next danger.

questions.prompt: How can you tell you are helping D1 rather than duplicating D1?
questions.explanation: Cover the middle attacker while D1 faces the carrier, then call when roles change; if both chase one puck, another lane is open.

questions.prompt: Who is the off-puck low threat?
questions.explanation: Gold 2 is the off-puck attacker across the middle near the net. Recheck that threat as the puck moves.

questions.prompt: Which two things should YOU keep in view?
questions.explanation: Check the off-puck threat and carrier repeatedly rather than watching only one.

questions.prompt: Arrange one off-puck coverage scan.

options.text: See whether D1 has puck-side lane

questions.explanation: Locate Gold 2, check D1’s pressure and adjust the net-side relationship. The position does not establish completed coverage.

questions.prompt: Move YOU across the middle to compare a position near Gold 2.
questions.explanation: The example is nearer Navy’s net than Gold 2 and changes sides across the middle. Gold 1 still owns the puck; check both threats and communicate coverage.

questions.prompt: Gold 2 cuts from the far-side low slot toward the net. What must YOU update?

options.text: The lane between Gold 2 and the Navy net
The old spot even if Gold 2 moves
Only Gold 1’s stick, not the low lane

questions.explanation: Gold 2’s movement changes the net-side lane, so YOU update the coverage relationship before looking back to Gold 1; if the lane closes, communicate the handoff.

questions.prompt: How can YOU check the puck without losing Gold 2?
questions.explanation: Seek a net-side relationship with Gold 2 while repeatedly checking the puck and communicating with D1. Do not leave Gold 2 between YOU and the net as a default rule.

questions.prompt: Which shown skater is closest to the loose rebound?
questions.explanation: D1 is the closest shown skater. The goalie is also nearby and is closer to the puck; proximity does not establish control.

questions.prompt: Which two cues shape your second job?

options.text: The original shooting lane, without checking Gold 2 or D1

questions.explanation: Gold 2 is another scoring threat while D1 approaches the rebound. Check both that route and the puck contest.

questions.prompt: Arrange one second-player rebound read.

options.text: Check D1’s approach and the goalie

questions.explanation: The closest skater is not automatically the winner. Check the goalie and opponent before deciding who contests and who covers.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a net-side cover position while D1 approaches the loose rebound.
questions.explanation: The target keeps YOU net-side of Gold 2 and leaves D1 room to contest the rebound; D1 is the closest shown skater to the loose puck, so control is unresolved.

questions.prompt: If D1 gains clear control, what should YOU reassess?

options.text: Whether Gold 2 remains the nearest uncovered attacker

questions.explanation: D1’s control changes the puck threat, so keep Gold 2 covered and prepare an outlet; if Gold 2 leaves, scan next lane.

questions.prompt: Why must a rebound read distinguish loose from controlled?
questions.explanation: A loose puck may require a contest or containment. Control changes the available actions; a goalie cover or official’s signal requires another reassessment.

questions.prompt: What happened to D1’s pinch?

options.text: It happened behind the left net

questions.explanation: Possession was lost, so priority moves from attack to recovery; if Navy regains it, update.

questions.prompt: Which two dangers should YOU read?

options.text: Gold 1’s route out of the zone
An assumed empty passing lane for Gold 1

questions.explanation: Gold 1 carries while Gold 2 offers inside support, so recover middle and communicate; an empty-looking wall lane does not prove Gold 1 has no pass.

questions.prompt: Arrange one failed-pinch recovery.
questions.explanation: Locate the new carrier, compare inside coverage and communicate the pressure job. Closing on Gold 1 is not automatically the next step.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward the middle while remaining closer to Navy’s net than Gold 2.
questions.explanation: The example stays net-side of Gold 2 but moves farther from Navy’s net than the starting spot. Check both attackers and D1 before choosing the route.

questions.prompt: If Gold 2 receives before you arrive, what is your priority?

options.text: Reassess Gold 2 as the carrier and coordinate net-side coverage

questions.explanation: The reception changes who can attack net, so switch scan and contain; if Gold 2 is covered, return to next threat.

questions.prompt: Why does the failed pinch change your next read?
questions.explanation: Gold now has possession. YOU are already net-side, so compare containment and support using both attackers and D1 rather than assuming a particular skating route.
